settings.label: Raw or cured
settings.somm_line: Raw and cured wants salinity and acid, not sugar. NON1 first — salt against brine — then NON2 if the plate leans savoury.

settings.label: Seafood
settings.somm_line: Fish needs a squeeze of citrus and a little salt. NON1 and NON2 do that from inside the glass.

settings.label: Vegetables
settings.somm_line: Vegetables lack the fat that makes wine easy to match, so salinity and bitterness do the work instead. NON2 and NON3 lead.

settings.label: Charred or roasted
settings.somm_line: Char wants tannin and something caramelised to meet it. NON3 for lighter plates, NON7 and NON9 when it is genuinely heavy.

settings.label: Braised
settings.somm_line: Slow-cooked fat needs cutting. NON5 if you want it sharp and sparkling, NON7 if you want it dark and bitter.

settings.label: Spice and heat
settings.somm_line: Alcohol amplifies capsaicin — this is the one advantage 0.0% has. NON5 is the coldest, saltiest, sharpest thing here.

settings.label: Cheese
settings.somm_line: Fat and salt with no cooking. NON3 has the grip; NON1 handles the fresh goat end of the board.

settings.label: Dessert
settings.somm_line: Sugar against sugar fails. NON3 and NON7 stay bitter enough to survive dessert.

settings.label: No food, just a glass
settings.somm_line: Nothing to match, so it only has to be sharp. NON5 is the lowest-sugar bottle on the shelf, NON1 the friendliest.
